stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ABC$?
stimulus: An astronomy student sketches lines between three stars, $A$, $B$, and $C$, to form triangle $ABC$. She then extends side $BC$ past $C$ to a point $D$, so that $B$, $C$, and $D$ lie on a line. In her sketch, the measure of angle $BAC$ is $48^\circ$ and the measure of angle $ACD$ is $115^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: $B$, $C$, and $D$ lie on a line, so angle $ACB$ and angle $ACD$ add to $180^\circ$. That makes angle $ACB = 180^\circ - 115^\circ = 65^\circ$. The angles of triangle $ABC$ add to $180^\circ$, so angle $ABC = 180^\circ - 48^\circ - 65^\circ = 67^\circ$. You can also use the exterior angle shortcut: $115^\circ - 48^\circ = 67^\circ$.

A.why: $65^\circ$ is angle $ACB$, the triangle's interior angle at $C$. You stopped after the straight-line step, before using the triangle sum to reach angle $ABC$.

C.why: $180^\circ - 48^\circ = 132^\circ$ is the combined measure of angles $ABC$ and $ACB$. You still need to subtract angle $ACB$ to get angle $ABC$ alone.

D.why: You added $115^\circ$ and $48^\circ$. The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, so the $48^\circ$ angle has to be subtracted from $115^\circ$, not added to it.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $PRT$?
stimulus: On a site map, an archaeologist draws two parallel wall foundations as line $\ell$ and line $m$. Point $P$ lies on line $\ell$, and point $S$ lies on line $\ell$ to the left of $P$. Points $Q$, $R$, and $T$ lie on line $m$ in that order from left to right. Survey trenches run along segments $PQ$ and $PR$. The measure of angle $SPQ$ is $74^\circ$ and the measure of angle $QPR$ is $38^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel, so angle $SPQ$ and angle $PQR$ are alternate interior angles. That makes angle $PQR = 74^\circ$. In triangle $PQR$, angle $PRQ = 180^\circ - 38^\circ - 74^\circ = 68^\circ$. Angle $PRT$ forms a straight line with angle $PRQ$, so angle $PRT = 180^\circ - 68^\circ = 112^\circ$.

A.why: $68^\circ$ is angle $PRQ$, the triangle's interior angle at $R$. The question asks for angle $PRT$, which is on the other side of $PR$ along line $m$, so you still need to subtract $68^\circ$ from $180^\circ$.

B.why: $74^\circ$ is angle $PQR$, the angle you carry across the parallel lines to $Q$. It is at a different vertex from angle $PRT$.

D.why: $180^\circ - 38^\circ = 142^\circ$ is the supplement of the triangle's angle at $P$, not an angle at $R$. You used the wrong vertex.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $EBF$?
stimulus: A printmaker cuts two straight grooves into a linoleum block. One groove runs along segment $AC$ and the other along segment $BD$, and they cross at point $E$. Point $F$ lies on the extension of segment $AB$ beyond $B$. The measure of angle $BAE$ is $52^\circ$ and the measure of angle $CED$ is $71^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Angles $AEB$ and $CED$ are vertical angles, so angle $AEB = 71^\circ$. In triangle $ABE$, angle $ABE = 180^\circ - 52^\circ - 71^\circ = 57^\circ$. Angle $EBF$ forms a straight line with angle $ABE$, so angle $EBF = 180^\circ - 57^\circ = 123^\circ$. This matches the exterior angle shortcut: $52^\circ + 71^\circ = 123^\circ$.

A.why: $57^\circ$ is angle $ABE$, the triangle's interior angle at $B$. Angle $EBF$ is the exterior angle beside it, so you needed one more step: subtract $57^\circ$ from $180^\circ$.

B.why: $71^\circ$ is angle $AEB$, the vertical partner of the given angle. It is an angle at $E$, not at $B$.

D.why: You treated angles $AEB$ and $CED$ as a linear pair and used $180^\circ - 71^\circ = 109^\circ$ in place of $71^\circ$. They are vertical angles, so they are equal.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $DAC$?
stimulus: A linguist draws a vowel chart as trapezoid $ABCD$, with side $AB$ parallel to side $DC$. A diagonal line along segment $AC$ splits the chart into two triangles. The measure of angle $ADC$ is $108^\circ$ and the measure of angle $BAC$ is $30^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: $AB$ is parallel to $DC$, and diagonal $AC$ crosses both, so angle $BAC$ and angle $DCA$ are alternate interior angles. That makes angle $DCA = 30^\circ$. In triangle $ADC$, angle $DAC = 180^\circ - 108^\circ - 30^\circ = 42^\circ$.

A.why: $30^\circ$ is angle $DCA$, which you get by carrying the given angle across the parallel sides. It is the middle step, not the angle at $A$ that the question asks for.

C.why: $180^\circ - 108^\circ = 72^\circ$ is the whole angle $DAB$ at corner $A$. The question asks only for the part on the $D$ side of the diagonal.

D.why: You found $180^\circ - 108^\circ = 72^\circ$ and then added $30^\circ$ when you should have subtracted it. The triangle sum leaves $72^\circ - 30^\circ$ for angle $DAC$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $FAK$?
stimulus: A sports scientist traces a sprinter's leg on a video frame. Line $j$ passes through the hip, $H$, and line $k$ passes through the ankle, $A$. The two lines are parallel. The thigh runs along segment $HK$ and the shin runs along segment $KA$, where the knee, $K$, lies between the two lines and to the right of both $H$ and $A$. Point $G$ lies on line $j$ to the right of $H$, and point $F$ lies on line $k$ to the left of $A$. The measure of angle $GHK$ is $40^\circ$ and the measure of angle $HKA$ is $75^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Draw a line through $K$ parallel to $j$ and $k$. That line splits angle $HKA$ into two parts. The upper part equals angle $GHK$ (alternate interior angles), so it is $40^\circ$. The lower part is $75^\circ - 40^\circ = 35^\circ$, and it equals the angle between $KA$ and line $k$ on the right of $A$. Angle $FAK$ is on the left of $A$ along the same line, so angle $FAK = 180^\circ - 35^\circ = 145^\circ$.

A.why: $35^\circ$ is the angle between the shin and line $k$ on the right of $A$. Angle $FAK$ opens to the left, so you still need to subtract $35^\circ$ from $180^\circ$.

B.why: You added $40^\circ$ and $75^\circ$. The $40^\circ$ angle is one part of the $75^\circ$ angle at the knee, so you should subtract it to find the other part.

C.why: $180^\circ - 40^\circ = 140^\circ$ is the angle between the thigh and line $j$ on the left of $H$. That is an angle at the hip, not the angle at the ankle that the question asks for.

stem: What is the value of $x$?
stimulus: In an astronomer's sketch of sight lines to three stars, segments $AD$ and $BE$ intersect at point $C$, forming triangle $ABC$. Angle $DCE$ measures $64^\circ$ and angle $CAB$ measures $71^\circ$. Side $AB$ is extended past $B$ to point $F$, and angle $CBF$ measures $x^\circ$.
explanation: Angles $ACB$ and $DCE$ are vertical angles, so angle $ACB$ measures $64^\circ$. Angle $CBF$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABC$ at $B$, so it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: $x = 71 + 64 = 135$.

A.why: You found $180 - 71 = 109$, which is the exterior angle at vertex $A$. The question asks for the exterior angle at $B$, which comes from the two interior angles at $A$ and $C$.

C.why: You found the interior angle $ABC = 180 - 71 - 64 = 45$ and stopped there. Angle $CBF$ is the linear pair of that angle, so it measures $180 - 45 = 135$.

D.why: You found $180 - 64 = 116$, which is the angle next to angle $ACB$ along segment $AD$. That angle is at $C$, not at $B$. Angle $DCE$ is vertical to angle $ACB$, so the two angles are equal, not supplementary.

stem: Which expression represents the measure, in degrees, of angle $ACD$?
stimulus: A harp maker sketches part of a frame. Lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel. Point $A$ is on line $\ell$, and points $B$, $C$, and $D$ are on line $m$, with $C$ between $B$ and $D$. Point $E$ is on line $\ell$, on the opposite side of line $AB$ from point $C$. Angle $EAB$ measures $x^\circ$, and angle $BAC$ measures $y^\circ$.
explanation: Line $AB$ is a transversal of the parallel lines, and $E$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of it. That makes angles $EAB$ and $ABC$ alternate interior angles, so angle $ABC$ measures $x^\circ$. Angle $ACD$ is the exterior angle of triangle $ABC$ at $C$. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, so its measure is $x + y$.

A.why: This is angle $ACB$, the interior angle of the triangle at $C$. You found it correctly but stopped there. The question asks for angle $ACD$, which is its supplement on line $m$.

C.why: You treated angles $EAB$ and $ABC$ as co-interior and gave angle $ABC$ as $180 - x$. Because $E$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of the transversal, the angles are alternate interior angles, so they are equal.

D.why: You used only the angle at $A$ and never moved $x$ across the parallel lines. The exterior angle at $C$ depends on both opposite interior angles, so $x$ has to appear in the answer.

stem: Which expression represents the measure, in degrees, of angle $OSR$?
stimulus: On a survey map, two straight canal banks run along lines $p$ and $q$, which intersect at point $O$. One of the angles formed at $O$ measures $a^\circ$. A weir runs from point $R$ on line $p$ to point $S$ on line $q$. Triangle $ORS$ lies inside the angle vertical to the $a^\circ$ angle, and angle $ORS$ measures $b^\circ$.
explanation: The triangle's angle at $O$ is vertical to the $a^\circ$ angle, so angle $ROS$ measures $a^\circ$. The angles of triangle $ORS$ sum to $180^\circ$, so angle $OSR$ measures $180 - a - b$.

A.why: This is the exterior angle of the triangle at $S$, the sum of the two opposite interior angles. The question asks for the interior angle $OSR$, which is the supplement of that exterior angle.

C.why: You took the triangle's angle at $O$ to be $180 - a$, the linear-pair partner of the given angle. The triangle sits in the vertical angle, so its angle at $O$ equals $a$. Using $180 - a$ gives $180 - b - (180 - a) = a - b$.

D.why: You used the angle at $O$ but left out angle $ORS$. The triangle sum needs all three angles, so $b$ also has to be subtracted.

stem: Which expression represents the measure, in degrees, of angle $DAB$?
stimulus: A paleobotanist traces the outline of a fossil leaf as quadrilateral $ABCD$, where side $AB$ is parallel to side $DC$. Diagonal $AC$ is drawn. Angle $BAC$ measures $x^\circ$, and angle $ADC$ measures $y^\circ$.
explanation: Diagonal $AC$ is a transversal of the parallel sides $AB$ and $DC$, so alternate interior angle $ACD$ also measures $x^\circ$. In triangle $ACD$, angle $DAC$ measures $180 - x - y$. Angle $DAB$ is made up of angles $DAC$ and $CAB$, so it measures $(180 - x - y) + x = 180 - y$.

A.why: This is angle $DAC$, only the part of angle $A$ inside triangle $ACD$. You still need to add angle $CAB$ to get the whole angle $DAB$.

B.why: You moved $x$ across the parallel sides to angle $ACD$ and then took its supplement on line $DC$. That angle sits at $C$, not at $A$, and the result never uses $y$.

D.why: You subtracted angle $DAC$ from $x$ when you should have added the two parts. $x - (180 - x - y)$ gives $2x + y - 180$, but angle $DAB$ is the sum of angles $DAC$ and $CAB$.

D.why: You took the supplement of $\angle QPR$ ($180 - 40$). That angle sits at $P$, not at $R$.

stem: How many degrees greater is the measure of angle $CAB$ than the measure of angle $ACB$?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
A materials scientist traces two straight cracks in a ceramic sample. In the figure, segments $AD$ and $BE$ intersect at point $C$. Segment $AB$ is drawn, which forms triangle $ABC$, and $AC = BC$. The measure of angle $DCE$ is $40^\circ$.
explanation: Angles $ACB$ and $DCE$ are vertical angles, so angle $ACB$ is $40^\circ$. Because $AC = BC$, the base angles $CAB$ and $CBA$ are equal, and each one is $\frac{180 - 40}{2} = 70^\circ$. The difference is $70 - 40 = 30$ degrees.

B.why: You gave the measure of angle $ACB$, which you get from the vertical angles. The question asks for the gap between two angles, not for either angle alone.

C.why: You stopped at the base angle $CAB$. You still needed to subtract the measure of angle $ACB$.

D.why: You added $70$ and $40$ when you should have subtracted. "How much greater" asks for a difference.

An ornithologist sketches a heron's flight between two parallel shorelines. In the figure, line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$, and line $\ell$ is above line $m$. Point $A$ is on line $\ell$ and point $B$ is on line $m$. Point $C$ is between the lines, to the right of both $A$ and $B$. Segments $AC$ and $BC$ are drawn, and point $D$ is on ray $AC$ beyond $C$. Point $P$ is on line $\ell$ to the right of $A$, and point $Q$ is on line $m$ to the right of $B$. The measure of angle $PAC$ is $35^\circ$ and the measure of angle $QBC$ is $50^\circ$.
explanation: Draw a line through $C$ parallel to $\ell$ and $m$. It splits angle $ACB$ into two parts. One part is alternate interior to angle $PAC$, so it is $35^\circ$. The other is alternate interior to angle $QBC$, so it is $50^\circ$. That makes angle $ACB = 35 + 50 = 85^\circ$. Angle $BCD$ forms a linear pair with angle $ACB$, so angle $BCD = 180 - 85 = 95^\circ$. The difference is $95 - 85 = 10$ degrees.

B.why: You subtracted the two given angles, $50 - 35$. The question compares angles $BCD$ and $ACB$ at point $C$, not the angles at the shorelines.

C.why: You stopped at angle $ACB$, which is only partway through the solution. You still needed its supplement, and then the gap between the two.

D.why: You found angle $BCD$ correctly but gave its measure. The question asks how much greater it is than angle $ACB$.
